Level 3 · Advanced · Week 7

Grids, Recursion and Fractal Art

Functions that call themselves; worlds made of grids.

What you will learn

  • What recursion is: a function that calls itself on a smaller problem.
  • Why every recursive function needs a base case.
  • How to store a game map or a picture in a grid (a list of lists).
  • How to draw a fractal tree and build a paint bucket tool.

The big idea: functions that call themselves

Open a Russian doll and you find a smaller doll. Open that one: an even smaller doll. You keep doing the same job until you reach the tiny solid doll – then you stop.

A recursive function works the same way. It has two parts:

  • the base case: the tiny problem you can answer straight away – stop here;

  • the recursive case: do one small step, then call yourself on a smaller problem.

countdown: a recursive function

def countdown(n):
    if n <= 0:            # base case: stop
        print("Liftoff!")
        return
    print(n)              # one small step
    countdown(n - 1)      # the same job on a smaller number

When you call countdown(3), Python stacks up the calls like plates. Each call waits for the smaller one to finish:

Bug huntNo base case = never-ending dolls

If you forget the base case, the function calls itself forever. Python stops it after about 1000 calls with RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded. When you see that error, look for the base case first. Also check that each call is on a smaller problem (n - 1, not n).

Predict! What does stars(3) print? Write it before you run it.

def stars(n):
    if n == 0:
        return
    print("*" * n)
    stars(n - 1)

Fractals: pictures made of smaller copies

A fractal is a shape made of smaller copies of itself. A tree is a trunk with two smaller trees on top. Each smaller tree is a trunk with two even smaller trees on top... until the depth reaches 0.

Grids: worlds made of rows

A grid is a list of rows, and each row is a list of cells. You find a cell with grid[row][col]: first go down to the row, then across to the column. Both start at 0.

You can make a grid from strings: grid = [list(row) for row in ["    ", " .T ", " .^ "]]. Change a cell with grid[2][1] = "T". The neighbors of a cell are the cells up, down, left and right of it (watch out for the edges!).

A paint bucket (flood fill) uses recursion on a grid: paint this cell, then ask each neighbor to do the same – but stop at the edge, at walls, and at cells you have already painted. Those are the base cases.

New words

recursion
When a function calls itself to solve a smaller copy of the same problem.
base case
The simplest case, answered without calling the function again. It stops the recursion.
recursive case
The part that does a small step and calls the function on a smaller problem.
RecursionError
Python’s error when a function calls itself too many times – usually a missing base case.
fractal
A shape made of smaller copies of itself, like a tree, a fern or a snowflake.
grid (2D list)
A list of rows, where each row is a list. grid[row][col] is one cell.
flood fill
Filling every touching cell of the same color, like a paint bucket tool.

Homework: Grids, Recursion and Fractal Art

15–20 minutes. Do Core first; Challenge and Creative are optional.

CoreTreasure map (about 10 minutes)

Open 3-advanced/exercises/week07/hw-treasure-map/starter.py in Thonny and press F5. The map is a grid: ~ water, ^ mountain, . grass, T treasure, S start.

  1. Finish count_tiles(grid, tile). Hint: a list has .count(), e.g. ["a", "b", "a"].count("a") is 2.

  2. Finish neighbors(grid, row, col): the cells up, down, left and right – but never off the edge of the map.

How many neighbors does a corner cell have? (blank to fill in) A cell in the middle? (blank to fill in)
